example: Project Blue Sky Inc v Australian Broadcasting Authority [1998] HCA 28
purpose: Test whether a typed graph can represent a bounded statutory interaction before attempting multi-jurisdiction legal topology.
research_note: Primary-source pinpoints have been added by AI research. Nothing in this file is HUMAN_VERIFIED until a human reviewer checks the sources and modelling choices.

nodes.label: Broadcasting Services Act 1992 (Cth) s 122
nodes.role: statutory command and power to determine program standards, including standards relating to Australian content
nodes.source_citation: Broadcasting Services Act 1992 (Cth) s 122(1)(a), (2)(b), (4); Project Blue Sky [1998] HCA 28 [79]-[81]

nodes.label: Broadcasting Services Act 1992 (Cth) s 160(d)
nodes.role: general statutory obligation requiring ABA functions to be performed consistently with Australia's treaty and bilateral-agreement obligations
nodes.source_citation: Broadcasting Services Act 1992 (Cth) s 160(d); Project Blue Sky [1998] HCA 28 [80]-[82]

nodes.label: Protocol on Trade in Services to ANZCERTA (1988), Arts 4 and 5(1)
nodes.role: market-access and national-treatment obligations requiring treatment of New Zealand persons and services no less favourable than Australian persons and services
nodes.source_citation: Protocol on Trade in Services to the Australia New Zealand Closer Economic Relations - Trade Agreement, Australian Treaty Series 1988 No 20, Arts 4 and 5(1); Project Blue Sky [1998] HCA 28 [82], [84]
nodes.authority_level: Treaty obligation; High Court application through s 160(d)

nodes.label: Clause 9, Australian Content Standard determined 15 December 1995
nodes.role: exercise/output of the ABA's statutory program-standard function imposing an Australian transmission quota
nodes.legal_effect_in_case: Held to have been made in breach of the Act and therefore unlawfully made, but not invalid merely because of the s 160 breach.

nodes.label: Project Blue Sky consequence-of-breach analysis
nodes.role: determines whether statutory non-compliance entails invalidity by asking whether invalidity was a purpose of the legislation

edges.comment: The making of an Australian-content standard was within the functions/powers granted to the ABA; the problem was the manner of exercise, not absence of power to make such a standard at all.

The joint majority described ss 122 and 160 as interlocking provisions, with s 160 directing how the s 122 function is carried out; the s 122 power must be exercised within the framework imposed by s 160.

Graph-semantic use of INCORPORATES only: s 160(d) gives the relevant international obligations operative significance as constraints on the ABA's performance of its functions. This does not assert general transformation of the treaty into directly enforceable domestic law.
edges.source_citation: Project Blue Sky [1998] HCA 28 [82]; Protocol Arts 4 and 5(1)

edges.comment: Breach of s 160 did not itself entail invalidity. The joint majority asked whether invalidity was a purpose of the legislation and concluded that acts done in breach of s 160 are not invalid, although the breach is unlawful.
